records.name: Nebraska
records.summary:
A gubernatorial executive order (August 30, 2023) narrows the legal definitions of 'male' and 'female', declares a person's biological sex fixed at birth, ends state recognition of transgender people, and backs single-sex spaces for bathrooms and changing rooms - mostly resident-facing, but it signals an administration willing to use state machinery against gender identity.

Below the national score 0.36.

sources.summary: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (publisher returns 403 to automated fetches); the underlying Hill report covers the governor signing an executive order narrowing the legal definitions of 'male' and 'female' and ending state recognition of transgender people.

Governor's office announcement: on Aug. 30, 2023 Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signed an executive order establishing the Women's Bill of Rights, making him the second U.S. governor to sign such an order 'declaring the biological definition of male and female.' The order backs single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms and changing rooms and states that a person's biological sex is defined at birth. Primary state-government source for Nebraska's sex-definition policy.

Legal-news report: Nebraska Executive Order No. 23-16 signed Aug. 30, 2023 defines the terms sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, stating there are biological differences between males and females in athletic abilities and safety that warrant sex-based segregation for some athletic, social and educational spaces. Reports that opponents questioned the order's scope and legality, and links the order text itself.

Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signed an executive order on Aug. 30, 2023 establishing a Women's Bill of Rights, declaring a 'biological definition of male and female' and detailing the distinctions state agencies must apply. Local Nebraska news confirmation of the signing date and content of the executive order this record is about.

records.name: Montana
records.summary:
Montana has passed laws that would grade among the country's worst — including a facility-use ban and a public-buildings bathroom ban — but state courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined them under the state constitution, leaving little of the anti-trans statutory book in force.

That makes Montana the anomaly of the 2026 legal-risk assessments: the only state whose risk grade was lowered — from 'worst laws' to 'high risk' — by cumulative court rulings and injunctions, in the February 2026 cycle. Statutory risk is high; enforcement risk is genuinely mixed.

sources.summary: July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment: Montana is flagged as a special case — it has passed laws that would normally place it among the worst states, but those laws have been repeatedly blocked or enjoined under the state constitution, improving its standing on the assessment's rubric (which ranks states by expert reading of bills on adult and youth restrictions).

National risk assessment update: Montana is the single state that improves in the 2026 rankings, because the state court system has repeatedly blocked or enjoined anti-trans laws under the state constitution; adult restrictions that were passed have not taken full effect. Youth-side picture remains unstable nationally (federal policy shifts and litigation).
